C005.subject: Information theory
C005.object: in ranked-choice voting systems, the channel capacity is lower than in plurality systems when voter preferences are multi-peaked
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Information theory in ranked-choice voting systems, the channel capacity is lower than in plurality systems when voter preferences are multi-peaked]

[PATH:empirical] Empirical analysis of ballot data from ranked-choice and plurality elections (e.g., San Francisco or Maine RCV elections) to compute Shannon entropy or channel capacity, comparing transmission of voter preference distributions under multi-peaked conditions. — Directly tests the hypothesis by measuring actual information throughput in real-world voting systems, controlling for preference structure.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical modeling using information-theoretic frameworks (e.g., by Nicolaisen, Tideman, or related work in social choice and communication theory) to derive channel capacity bounds for ranked-choice and plurality systems under multi-peaked preference profiles. — Provides formal mathematical confirmation or refutation of the claimed capacity difference, independent of empirical noise.

[PATH:literature] Literature review of computational voting theory papers (e.g., from AAAI or EC conferences) that simulate multi-peaked preferences and compare information loss in ranked-choice vs. plurality systems using metrics like mutual information or distortion. — Synthesizes existing simulation results to assess whether the hypothesis is supported or contradicted by prior computational experiments.

qualifier.geographic: representative democracies with plurality or ranked voting systems

C006.subject: Information theory
C006.object: the complexity and nuances of electoral systems beyond simplistic models
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Information theory the complexity and nuances of electoral systems beyond simplistic models]

[PATH:empirical] Empirical study comparing Shannon entropy measures of voter preference distributions across different single-winner plurality systems (e.g., UK, US, Canada) to actual election outcomes and representation quality metrics — Directly tests whether information-theoretic metrics can capture non-simplistic electoral dynamics like strategic voting, gerrymandering, and third-party spoiler effects, providing evidence for or against the hypothesis.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical analysis of extensions to information theory (e.g., transfer entropy, mutual information in networked voter models) applied to electoral systems with multi-dimensional preference spaces and non-linear aggregation rules — Explores whether modified information-theoretic frameworks can overcome the limitations of simplistic models, potentially refuting the claim that information theory 'cannot' be directly applied.

[PATH:literature] Literature review of prior attempts to use information theory in electoral system analysis (e.g., works by Balinski & Young, or recent computational social choice papers) focusing on documented failures or successes in capturing complexity — Synthesizes existing evidence to assess whether the hypothesis is supported by historical application attempts, identifying systematic gaps or counterexamples.

qualifier.geographic: in representative democracies with single-winner plurality voting

C007.subject: Democratic deliberation and iterative voting
C007.predicate: fail to overcome when deliberation is constrained by time pressure
C007.object: the epistemic limitations imposed by the channel capacity of a single election round
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Democratic deliberation and iterative voting the epistemic limitations imposed by the channel capacity of a single election round]

[PATH:empirical] Laboratory experiment comparing iterative voting with 10-minute deliberation rounds vs. unrestricted deliberation, measuring preference convergence and collective accuracy — Directly tests whether time-constrained deliberation fails to improve epistemic outcomes beyond a single round, by manipulating deliberation duration and observing changes in group decision quality.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical analysis of information aggregation in multi-round voting under bounded communication (e.g., Landemore's epistemic democracy framework combined with channel capacity models) — Formalizes the claim that short deliberation rounds cannot transmit enough information to overcome the channel capacity limit of a single election, providing a mathematical basis for the hypothesis.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing studies on deliberation time and decision quality in participatory budgeting or citizen juries — Synthesizes prior empirical work to assess whether time-pressured deliberation consistently fails to improve epistemic outcomes, offering indirect evidence for or against the hypothesis.

qualifier.condition: when each deliberation round is limited to less than 10 minutes and voters cannot revise preferences after the first round

C008.subject: Democratic deliberation and iterative voting
C008.object: the inherent biases and structural inequalities in voter participation
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Democratic deliberation and iterative voting the inherent biases and structural inequalities in voter participation]

[PATH:empirical] Field experiments on deliberative polling and voter turnout disparities (e.g., Fishkin & Luskin, 2005; more recent replications) — Directly tests whether iterative deliberation reduces or fails to mitigate socioeconomic and racial biases in participation, providing causal evidence on the hypothesis.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of iterative voting mechanisms and inequality outcomes (e.g., studies on sequential voting in multi-round elections, such as French presidential elections or US primaries) — Synthesizes existing evidence on whether repeated voting cycles amplify or counteract structural inequalities (e.g., resource-driven drop-off, polarization), offering a broad empirical basis.

[PATH:theoretical] Formal model of iterative deliberation under asymmetric information and power (e.g., extensions of Austen-Smith & Feddersen, 2006) — Models whether deliberation and repeated voting can overcome inherent biases given unequal resources or status, clarifying necessary conditions and limits for the hypothesis.

qualifier.geographic: Western liberal democracies with established multi-round voting procedures
